title: Directory of Catechesis

toc.t: The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis
Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End
The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists

notes: John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution “Fidei Depositum” I

For our Institute the Catechism of the Catholic Church will be a valuable instrument, since it has been known as an “organic exposition of all the Catholic Faith” (CI 18), of an understanding of the four pillars: baptismal profession of faith, the sacraments of the faith, the life of faith, and prayer of the believer (cf. CI 13).   This catechism constitutes a service that the successor of Peter wants to give to the Holy Catholic Church, in order to support and confirm the faith of all the disciples of the Lord, as bonds of unity in the same apostolic faith.
St. Thomas Aquinas, Super Epistolam ad Ephesios, III, 4. (Translated from Spanish)
Catechism of the Council of Trent (CR), Preface.  Translation by Rev. J. Donovan, 1829.
In this work the parish priest will be helped by his assistants.

html:
Directory of Catechesis

Introduction

“Jesus did and taught (Acts 1:1). Therefore, in our spirituality we should never dialectically separate teaching from work or work from teaching. It is always necessary to unite integrity of doctrine with rectitude of life, orthodoxy with orthopraxis. In all of revelation word and work – dabar and barah – are inseparably united.”1

“We will devote ourselves especially to preaching the Word of God... in all its forms by studying and teaching Sacred Scripture... [and] catechisis,”2 participating in the prophetic office of Christ.3

As a Congregation, we must have always present the words of the Holy Father to religious: “I wholeheartedly exhort you, whose religious consecration should make you even more readily available for the Church's service, to prepare as well as possible for the task of catechesis according to the differing vocations of your institutes and the missions entrusted to you, and to carry this concern everywhere. Let the communities dedicate as much as possible of what ability and means they have to the specific work of catechesis.”4

To dedicate all of our energies in this work we must also be interiorly convicted that: “The more the Church, whether on the local or the universal level, gives catechesis priority… the more she finds in catechesis a strengthening of her internal life as a community of believers and of her external activity as a missionary Church. As the 20th century draws to a close, the Church is bidden by God and by events - each of them a call from Him - to renew her trust in catechetical activity as a prime aspect of her mission. She is bidden to offer catechesis her best resources in people and energy, without sparing effort, toil or material means, in order to organize it better and to train qualified personnel. This is no mere human calculation; it is an attitude of faith. And an attitude of faith always has reference to the faithfulness of God, who never fails to respond.” 5

We will develop… the essential elements that we will have to have in mind in order to complete this fundamental mission that the Church has entrusted to us. To do this we have tried to respond to the questions: What is catechesis and its history in the Church? What should be the content of catechesis? How ought one organize and present this material? How must we transmit this material? Who should teach catechesis? How should catechists be prepared? Who will be the addressees of such teaching? What are the demands of a catechesis that truly begins in “the life in Christ”?

We have taken our exposition of these points from the abundance of that magnificent document of John Paul II, the encyclical Catechesi Tradendae. We also have always had present the Catechism of the Catholic Church.

Part I

The Urgency and Necessity of Catechesis

The principal urgency and necessity of catechesis derive from the mandate that Jesus Christ Himself gave before His Ascension: “Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Mt 28:19-20).

The Roman Catechism of the Council of Trent tells us in the first section for parish priests that “man, abandoned to his own power, can attain neither true wisdom nor sure means of attaining happiness.” From this we see the need for catechesis so that man can effectively reach his end. We ought to put into practice what is expressed in the Constitutions: “They will work so that the principles of the Gospel effectively influence the lives of men…and they will combat error with all their strength.”6

On the other hand the pressing reality that the contemporary world presents shows us that: “Today, the human race is involved in a new stage of history. Profound and rapid changes are spreading by degrees around the whole world. … Hence we can already speak of a true cultural and social transformation, one which has repercussions on man's religious life as well,”7 resulting in the generation of distinct problems:

the cultural tradition was more favorable in the past than it is today for the transmission of the faith;

in order that the Christian faith profoundly penetrates cultures not yet evangelized, new forms of expression are needed, as long as the fundamental postulations remain the same;

pluralism and moral relativism reign in society;

also, there is a growing indifferentism on the part of persons;

and the enslavement of the means of communication, to the point that “in particular, the younger generation is growing up in a world conditioned by the mass media.”8

This dynamism proper to our time should in no way regulate the principles of the Christian faith; to the contrary, it ought to urge us to make an analysis of this reality in order to show to men the danger that encircles them and the solution that the Gospel message proposes to us; for this we must “assume the responsibility of teaching catechism to children and adults.”9

Part II

Object of the Directory: Catechesis

We do not find in the New Testament the noun “catechesis,” but we do find the verb “katechein” with the ordinary sense of “to tell”, “to instruct”, “to teach” in a religious sense.10 Such was the catechesis in the first Christian community and, in this sense, it is clear that the primitive Church was born from the teaching of the faith and from the catechesis done by the Apostles, because, “How can they believe in Him of Whom they have not heard?”11

The fundamental importance of the theme is evident since it treats of the transmission of the doctrine of the faith. “The Church has always considered catechesis one of her primary tasks, for, before Christ ascended to His Father after His resurrection, He gave the Apostles a final command - to make disciples of all nations and to teach them to observe all that He had commanded.12”13

“Very soon the name of catechesis was given to the whole of the efforts within the Church to make disciples, to help people to believe that Jesus is the Son of God, so that believing they might have life in His name,14 and to educate and instruct them in this life and thus build up the Body of Christ. The Church has not ceased to devote her energy to this task.”15

“Some of the most impressive Bishops and pastors, especially in the third and fourth centuries considered it an important part of their episcopal ministry to deliver catechetical instructions and write treatises. It was the age of Cyril of Jerusalem and John Chrysostom, of Ambrose and Augustine, the age that saw the flowering, from the pen of numerous Fathers of the Church, of works that are still models for us.”16

The Councils were always a fount of energy for catechesis. We ought to remember the Council of Trent and its Roman Catechism, and in particular, as a fruit of Vatican II, The Catechism of the Catholic Church, a providential gift for our times. On this point, the Holy Father expressed that: “Following the renewal of the Liturgy and the new codification of the canon law of the Latin Church and that of the Oriental Catholic Churches, this catechism will make a very important contribution to that work of renewing the whole life of the Church, as desired and begun by the Second Vatican Council.”17

John Paul II asks “the Church's Pastors and the Christian faithful to receive this catechism in a spirit of communion and to use it assiduously in fulfilling their mission of proclaiming the faith and calling people to the Gospel life. This catechism is given to them that it may be a sure and authentic reference text for teaching Catholic doctrine and particularly for preparing local catechisms.”18

Also bear in mind the General Directory for Catechesis promoted by the Sacred Congregation for the Clergy, since it : “provides the basic principles of pastoral theology taken from the Magisterium of the Church, and in a special way from the Second Vatican Council by which pastoral action in the ministry of the word can be more fittingly directed and governed. Both instruments [the Catechism of the Catholic Church and the General Directory for Catechesis], each taken in accordance with its specific nature and authority, are mutually complementary.”19

Thus, in a specific sense, “All in all, it can be taken here that catechesis is an education of children, young people and adults in the faith, which includes especially the teaching of Christian doctrine imparted, generally speaking, in an organic and systematic way, with a view to initiating the hearers into the fullness of Christian life.”20

Part III

The Content of Catechesis

With regard to the content of the faith that is transmitted in catechesis, it is clear that it concerns the unique message of eternal salvation that directs all men of all cultures and of all times. The respect for the integrity of this content is the indispensable condition of Catholic catechesis. “In order that the sacrificial offering of his or her faith (cf. Phil 2:17) should be perfect, the person who becomes a disciple of Christ has the right to receive "the word of faith"(Rom 10:8) not in mutilated, falsified or diminished form, but whole and entire, in all its rigor and vigor. … Thus, no true catechist can lawfully, on his own initiative, make a selection of what he considers important in the deposit of faith as opposed to what he considers unimportant, so as to teach the one and reject the other.”21

“A catechism should faithfully and systematically present the teaching of Sacred Scripture, the living Tradition in the Church and the authentic Magisterium, as well as the spiritual heritage of the Fathers, Doctors, and saints of the Church, to allow for a better knowledge of the Christian mystery and for enlivening the faith of the People of God. It should take into account the doctrinal statements which the Holy Spirit has intimated to his Church down the centuries. It should help to illumine with the light of faith the new situations and problems which had not yet emerged in the past.”22 23

All catechetical formation must include a liturgical aspect. The same sacred signs are a fountain of catechetical formation. “Catechesis is intrinsically bound to every liturgical and sacramental action. Frequently however, the practice of catechetics testifies to a weak and fragmentary link with the liturgy: limited attention to liturgical symbols and rites, scant use of the liturgical fonts, catechetical courses with little or no connection with the liturgical year; [and] the marginalization of liturgical celebrations in catechetical programs.”24

Part IV

How to Teach Catechesis

“Catechetical instruction is to be given by using all helps, teaching aids, and instruments of social communication which seem more effective so that the faithful, in a manner adapted to their character, capabilities and age, and conditions of life, are able to learn Catholic doctrine more fully and put it into practice more suitably.”25

We must pay attention to two poles: the means to use and the diversity of those we will teach.

Chapter 1: The Means in Service of the End

In the catechetical field there is not one unique method of transmitting revealed truth. One must have in mind that “The end is always higher than the things that are ordered to it.”26 Therefore be attentive to utilize in the transmission of the faith all the suitable means for its best understanding and dissemination; just as one makes sure that a particular method of writing a catechism, or of explaining it, does not result in harm to the contents that one wants to teach or for the end that the catechesis proposes with this teaching. This harm not only has repercussions in scientific errors, but also in something that is graver: the salvation of souls. Therefore, to refer to the means that the catechist has to employ, the General Directory for Catechesis says that one has to use that which is best for obtaining the spiritual ends that one pursues.

The election of methods, then, will be valid “to the extent that far from being dictated by more or less subjective theories or prejudices stamped with a certain ideology, it is inspired by the humble concern to stay closer to a content that must remain intact.”27 If not, it will fall into the vanity of which St. Thomas spoke, since “a man is called vain who, lead by a wrong rule, does not reach the right end.”28

Catechesis is to form the faith of children, youth, and adults, by means of an organic and systematic instruction, aiming at initiating them into the fullness of Christian life.29

We must categorically affirm, therefore, that catechesis “must be systematic, not improvised but programmed to reach a precise goal; it must deal with essentials, without any claim to tackle all disputed questions or to transform itself into theological research or scientific exegesis; it must nevertheless be sufficiently complete, not stopping short at the initial proclamation of the Christian mystery such as we have in the kerygma; [and] it must be an integral Christian initiation, open to all the other factors of Christian life.”30

After this very clear affirmation, the Holy Father stressed anew “the need for organic and systematic Christian instruction, because of the tendency in various quarters to minimize its importance.”31 And he sums up those tendencies, disqualifying them with all clarity: “It is useless to play off orthopraxis against orthodoxy: Christianity is inseparably both. … It is also quite useless to campaign for the abandonment of serious and orderly study of the message of Christ in the name of a method concentrating on life experience. … Nor is any opposition to be set up between a catechesis taking life as its point of departure and a traditional doctrinal and systematic catechesis. Authentic catechesis is always an orderly and systematic initiation into the revelation that God has given of Himself to humanity in Christ Jesus, a revelation stored in the depths of the Church's memory and in Sacred Scripture, and constantly communicated from one generation to the next by a living, active tradition. This revelation is not however isolated from life or artificially juxtaposed to it. It is concerned with the ultimate meaning of life and it illumines the whole of life with the light of the Gospel, to inspire it or to question it.”32

The desire to spread the faith in order that it become more alive and efficacious in men, will lead, of course, to utilizing all the resources that the discoveries of human sciences offer. “In fact, it is natural that techniques perfected and tested for education in general should be adapted for the service of education in the faith. However, account must always be taken of the absolute originality of faith. Pedagogy of faith is not a question of transmitting human knowledge, even of the highest kind; it is a question of communicating God's revelation in its entirety. Throughout sacred history, especially in the Gospel, God Himself used a pedagogy that must continue to be a model for the pedagogy of faith.”33

The most elementary of whatever catechetical system and method, to our understanding, must have in mind the following:

it must expound in simple and appropriate language the essentials of the deposit of the faith;

this exposition of the deposit of the faith must be done in an ordered way, in order to show the necessary connections existing between the truths of the faith;

it must make sure that the fundamentals of the faith be memorized, since they will live the rest of their life a good part of Christians;

and, through these truths, it must move each person to rectify his conduct, by an exacting application of the faith to all the circumstances of his life, whether in his relationship with God directly, or in all his human relationships, that have to be also dealt with God.

Chapter 2: The Addressees of Catechesis

The diversity of persons to which catechism is directed demands a necessary adaptation in all cases.

“He who instructs [should] become all things to all men (1 Cor 9:22), and be able to gain all to Christ. …Nor let him imagine that those committed to his care are of all equal capacity or like dispositions, so as to enable him to apply the same course of instruction, to lead all to knowledge and piety; for some are, “as it were new-born infants,” others grown up in Christ, and others in some sort, of full maturity. …all who are called to this ministry [should] understand that in announcing the mysteries of faith and in inculcating the precepts of morality, the instruction is to be accommodated to the capacity and intelligence of the hearers.”34

“The age and the intellectual development of Christians, their degree of ecclesial and spiritual maturity and many other personal circumstances demand that catechesis should adopt widely differing methods for the attainment of its specific aim: education in the faith. On a more general level, this variety is also demanded by the social and cultural milieu in which the Church carries out her catechetical work.”35

Nevertheless, one must always remember in choosing a method and the most suitable language to use, that “the choice made will be a valid one to the extent that, far from being dictated by more or less subjective theories or prejudices stamped with a certain ideology, it is inspired by the humble concern to stay closer to a content that must remain intact. The method and language used must truly be means for communicating the whole and not just a part of ‘the words of eternal life’ ( Jn. 6:69; cf. Acts 5:20; 7:38) and the ‘ways of life’ (Acts 2:28, quoting Ps. 16:11).”36

In this work of necessary adaptation, “the first question of a general kind that presents itself here concerns the danger and the temptation to mix catechetical teaching unduly with overt or masked ideological views, especially political and social ones, or with personal political options.”37 The catechist must always stand firm over these unilateral options and for him, “it is on the basis of revelation that catechesis will try to set its course, revelation as transmitted by the universal Magisterium of the Church, in its solemn or ordinary form.”38

Another great challenge for catechesis is the incarnation of the message in cultures. “We can say of catechesis, as well as of evangelization in general, that it is called to bring the power of the Gospel into the very heart of culture and cultures. For this purpose, catechesis will seek to know these cultures and their essential components… and help them to bring forth, from their own living tradition, original expressions of Christian life, celebration and thought.”39 In this work one must remember that “on the one hand the Gospel message cannot be purely and simply isolated from the culture in which it was first inserted…nor…the cultures in which it has already been expressed down the centuries. On the other hand, the power of the Gospel everywhere transforms and regenerates. When that power enters into a culture, it is no surprise that it rectifies many of its elements. There would be no catechesis if it were the Gospel that had to change when it came into contact with the cultures.”40 One of the works with which our Institute can collaborate in this infusion of the Gospel into cultures will be the translation, publication, diffusion and teaching of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, especially in the places of mission.

Part V

Who Ought to Teach

“It is a proper and grave duty especially of pastors of souls to take care of the catechesis of the Christian people so that the living faith of the faithful becomes manifest and active through doctrinal instruction and the experience of Christian life.”41

In the first place, the exhortation of the Holy Father in Catechesi Tradendae direcs the bishops whose principal commitment must be “to bring about and maintain” in the local churches a “a real passion for catechesis, a passion embodied in a pertinent and effective organization, putting into operation the necessary personnel, means and equipment, and also financial resources.”42

Then the Holy Father tells the priests how to immediately assist the bishops: “with all my strength I beg you, ministers of Jesus Christ: Do not, for lack of zeal or because of some unfortunate preconceived idea, leave the faithful without catechesis. Let it not be said that ‘the children beg for food, but no one gives to them’ (Lam 4:4).”43

“By virtue of his function, a pastor is bound to take care of the catechetical formation of adults, youth, and children, to which purpose he is to use the help of the clerics attached to the parish, of members of institutes of consecrated life and of societies of apostolic life, taking into account the character of each institute, and of lay members of the Christian faithful, especially of catechists.”44

Thus, the Holy Father entrusts catechesis to religious and to the faithful laity, and then reminds us of most excellent place for catechesis: the Parish. We must be convinced that the center of catechesis is the Parish and the parish priest must consider it as one of his most important responsibilities. “It is true that catechesis can be given anywhere, but I wish to stress…that the parish community must continue to be the prime mover and preeminent place for catechesis.”45 An adequate catechesis, in its different levels, especially for children, constitutes the central apostolate of the Parish. And it is precisely the parish that must promote the great work of catechesis in families, in schools and in the movements of the faithful, etc.

Keep in mind what our Constitutions say: “Religious who assist in parishes should give priority, in an enthusiastic pastoral action, to the…responsibility of teaching catechism to children and adults.”46 47

Inasmuch as the faithful laity do not encounter legitimate impediments, “parents above others are obliged to form their children by word and example in faith and in the practice of Christian life; sponsors and those who take the place of parents are bound by an equal obligation.”48

This right that parents posses cannot enter into conflict with the responsibility conferred by the Church on legitimate pastors who are in charge of organizing and keeping watch over catechesis. “Family catechesis precedes, accompanies, and enriches other forms of instruction in the faith. Parents have the mission of teaching their children to pray and to discover their vocation as children of God. The parish is the Eucharistic community and the heart of the liturgical life of Christian families; it is a privileged place for the catechesis of children and parents.”49

Make use of the various means of social communication: bulletins and newsletters, reviews and magazines, radio or television programs, videos, etc… by these, catechism can reach more people, environments, families…

Part VI

The Necessary Preparation of the Catechists

The great Spanish catechist, Mons. Manuel González, sums up this important question on the necessary intellectual and spiritual preparation of catechists in one principle and three proverbs.

First of all, the principle: “Catechesis is the catechist.” He explains: “Give me a catechist with vocation…, with adequate intellectual preparation, who treats first with the Heart of Jesus in the Sanctuary, who next treats with children and who, above all, loves these children with the love drawn from the Sanctuary, give me a catechist like this and do not tell me that this catechist cannot teach, cannot do his job, because he lacks educational material like posters, projectors, valuable rewards, attractive outings, etc. This catechist that you have described will be able to manage so that the expressions of his face and the form and contortions of his body substitute for and surpass posters or projectors, and will give great value to and more than make up for, with his smile and his warm word, the affection, trinket or trifle of which in his poverty he prepares for prizes. In other words, the problem of Christian instruction and education of the people, more than a problem of laws, of organization, or of works, is a problem of man.”

And in three proverbs, he leaves us fundamental pedagogical principles which sum up the most important things to take into account in catechesis with children, as in all catechesis.50

a) “No one gives what he does not have.” “Whoever does not possess Jesus cannot give Jesus.” Whoever wants to give to his students the clear and exact knowledge of Jesus Christ and His doctrine must, before all, posses such knowledge through responsible study and prayer. Whoever wants to transmit the liking and love for that which he teaches must begin by the imitation of the same. And finally, if the catechist wishes the children to come with enthusiasm to the doctrine, “to listen attentively to him with happiness and without fear or dissipation or disturbance, and to go with a desire to return,” he must begin by teaching in this way. If the catechist does not carry out these conditions, now he knows the cause of his failures.

b) “Children are children.” The catechist must exert himself to adapt his teaching to the age and condition of the students and cannot expect from them what they cannot give. Thus, for example, he cannot ask the seriousness and immobility of a class of adults from a class of children.

c) “Eyes that don’t see, heart that does not feel.” “While children see and understand better that which is explained to them, then their hearts will be more interested and will more deeply understand what is being taught.” For him, Mons. Manuel González proposes: “Give them more Sacred History or Gospels than lessons from the catechism text. Seek that they know first who is Jesus, what He did, where He lived and what He taught with His word. The holier the ideas, the more necessary it is to understand them thoroughly in order to love them. It is enough to know a good person a little in order to love him/her. It has been disgracefully forgotten that those who know more Theology are not necessarily better Christians, but those who more firmly believe and more loyally unite themselves to and love Jesus.”

Local superiors and especially parish priests (and their assistants) should pay close attention to the formation of catechists through fruitful participation in the Sunday Liturgy, courses, Spiritual Exercises, etc.

Pay special attention to promoting, supporting, and collaborating with all the initiatives on the diocesan level by starting schools or institutions for theological formation for laity, seeking that which imparts a competent catechesis. If such an institute of this nature already exists, offer members of our Religious Family to collaborate in it.

Part VII

To Whom Catechesis is Directed

“Attentive to the norms established by the diocesan bishop, a pastor is to take care in a special way:

that suitable catechesis is imparted for the celebration of the sacraments;

that through catechetical instruction imparted for an appropriate period of time, children are prepared properly for the first reception of the sacraments of penance and the Most Holy Eucharist and for the sacrament of confirmation;

that having received first communion, these children are enriched more fully and deeply through catechetical formation;

that catechetical instruction is given also to those who are physically or mentally impeded, insofar as their condition permits;

that the faith of youth and adults is strengthened, enlightened, and developed through various means and endeavors.”51

If we consider catechesis as the initiation into the sacramental life of the Church, according to the distinct conditions of the students, we must take into account in our parishes:

a) Catechism for children in First Communion and Confirmation classes

From infancy, the child should receive an organic formation in the faith. It is the stage of the student, the stage of cementing vital principles, of direction by parents, godparents, and catechists, of sowing good seeds on fertile soil.

Therefore, systematic or gradual catechesis is a fount of inspiration and formation in the faith and religiosity of children. It is a means of forming persons, directing moral criteria, and cultivating virtues.

In First Communion classes, teach them the principal mysteries of the faith and prepare them for a fruitful reception of the sacraments of Confession and Eucharist.

Prepare the children and adolescents who will receive the sacrament of Confirmation so that they not only strengthen their faith but also can defend it and proclaim it with works and words.

In our time it is common that children find themselves abandoned, suffer a spiritual abandonment, and even are abandoned by their own parents. In addition, the culture of death seeks to take away from them the most valuable thing they possess, the grace of God.

The work of the one dedicated to the apostolate with children must help them to grow spiritually so that they become saints, that is to say that they know and love Jesus very much. “Central aspects of the formation of children are training in prayer and introduction to Sacred Scripture”52

We should note some of the characteristics of children with their negative and positive aspects:

Negative aspects:

Take into account the influence of television. The images, music, and words strongly impress in sensibility of children that do not yet have critical judgment. Television increases the activity of the senses, diminishes intellectual activity, and conditions the conduct of the child. In addition, TV and video games impedes their ability to dedicate themselves to an activity that requires more attention, such as lectures or talks.

Take into account that familial problems, including broken families, the absence of the father or mother, etc. make it difficult for children to understand the paternity of God.

Patience must be practiced to the extreme because of the crisis of authority that exists today, in order to discover the best way to speak to children.

Positive aspects:

The generosity of children enables them to give that which to them is most precious. They are simple, unsophisticated, natural, without complications; they do not suffer from the miseries of grown-ups; they do not act with duplicity or hypocrisy.

In order to succeed in this, encourage the preaching of retreats for children, penitential para-liturgies, Masses for children with preaching themes adapted for them, popular missions, etc.

For the perseverance of children and youth, encourage oratories.

b) Catechesis for youth

The age of youth is very rich in dynamisms that strongly drive them to action. It is necessary to discover through this dynamism the values that move youth, for example, the search for security, authenticity, conquering self, relationships with others, service…

It is necessary to further orient them in the discovery of their vocation and of their cultivation. Implement a vocational catechesis, presenting the ideals of consecrated life as well as those of the matrimonial life.

In this age, youth demand a solid foundation in the faith, not so much with apologetical demonstrations, but rather the testimony of the Christian life which is capable of loving in truth and of radiating this love.

In this age, catechesis must be achieved by means of the dynamics of groups, in which an authentic friendship and spirituality provide youth with a real experience of Christian unity, founded on the charity of Christ.

We must also have systematic catechetical formation which should occupy the first place in the schools of our Institute. The principal object of our educational Institutes is the formation of good Christians; without this, they are meaningless.

We should be aware of different religious situations: unbaptized youth, baptized youth who have not been catechized or completed their Christian initiation, youth who encounter a crisis of faith, oftentimes grave, others who might have the option of faith, or others who have made an act of faith and hope to be helped.

Useful means for an efficacious catechesis include: a well oriented community action group, educational youth associations, and personal accompaniment of the youth, in which spiritual direction is highlighted.

One of the greatest difficulties that is confronted and should be responded to is the difference in language (mentality, sensibility, likes, style, vocabulary) between the youth and the Church (catechesis and catechists). It is important to insist on the necessity of an adaptation of catechesis to youth, knowing how to translate the message of Jesus Christ into their language “with patience and good will, without betraying it.”

Take advantage of the invitations given to members of our Religious Family to give talks in state or secular schools.

c) Catechism for adults

“From infancy until the threshold of maturity, catechesis is thus a permanent school of the faith and follows the major stages of life, like a beacon lighting the path of the child, the adolescent and the young person.”53 Also adults, since “for catechesis to be effective, it must be permanent, and it would be quite useless if it stopped short at the threshold of maturity, since catechesis, admittedly under another form, proves no less necessary for adults.”54

It should form Christians of enlightened faith, firm and faithfully lived, that is to say, capable of fully assuming life in all its realism, with its responsibilities and duties, in all the fields of human activity.

In particular the duties of catechesis with adults are:

Promote formation and maturation of life in the spirit of the resurrected Christ, with adequate means like sacramental pedagogy, retreats, and spiritual direction.

Educate in order to be able to objectively judge the socio-cultural changes of our society in the light of faith.

Give response to religious and moral questions of today (eg: public and individual morals).

Form them to assume responsibilities in the mission of the Church and to know how to give Christian testimony in society.

When dealing with adults who haven’t even received the sacraments, propose to them, by means of a prudently adapted catechesis, the necessary aids for them to receive them. They will them try to continue their formation.

d) Catechesis for the elderly

“Not infrequently the old are seen as passive objects and possibly even as an encumbrance. In the light of faith, however, they must be understood as a gift of God to the Church and to society, and must also be given adequate catechetical care. In catechesis, they have the same rights and duties as all Christians. … Catechesis for the aged pays particular attention to certain aspects of their condition of faith. An aged person may have a rich and solid faith, in which case catechesis, in a certain sense, brings to fulfillment a journey of faith in an attitude of thanksgiving and hopeful expectation. Others live a faith weakened by poor Christian practice. In this case, catechesis becomes a moment of new light and religious experience. Sometimes people reach old age profoundly wounded in body and soul. In these circumstances, catechesis can help them to live their condition in an attitude of prayer, forgiveness and inner peace. At any rate, the condition of the old calls for a catechesis of hope, which derives from the certainty of finally meeting God.”55

e) Catechesis for the sick

Those who have the apostolate with the sick should instruct them on the substantial reason for sufferings and on the justifications of the present condition, about the medicinal and expiatory value of the cross. Teach them also to participate through their sufferings in the great apostolate of the parish and of the Church. Encourage them to exercise themselves in patience and to prepare themselves for eternity.56

f) Catechesis for the handicapped

Take special care of these. “Every Christian community considers those who suffer handicaps, physical or mental, as well as other forms of disability—especially children—as persons particularly beloved of the Lord. A growth in social and ecclesial consciousness, together with undeniable progress in specialized pedagogy, makes it possible for the family and other formative centers to provide adequate catechesis for these people, who, as baptized, have this right and, if non-baptized, because they are called to salvation. … [This catechesis] is most effectively carried out in the context of the integral education of the person. On the other hand, the risk must be avoided of separating this specialized catechesis from the general pastoral care of the community. … The particular demands of this catechesis require a special competence from catechists and render their service all the more deserving.”57

We should give privileged attention to the sick and handicapped, for in them we discover the face of the suffering Christ.

Part VIII

Catechesis and Life in Christ

We reproduce a magnificent and rich text of the Catechism of the Catholic Church which gives us a summary of that which catechesis ought to be in order not to remain in the letter “which kills” but that introduces one truly into the mystery of the divine life which the Son of God has come to transmit to us by His Incarnation.

Catechesis has to reveal in all clarity the joy and the demands of the way of Christ (cf. CT 29). Catechesis for the “newness of life” in him (cf. Rom. 6:4) should be:

“a) a catechesis of the Holy Spirit, the interior Master of life according to Christ, a gentle guest and friend who inspires, guides, corrects, and strengthens this life;

“b) a catechesis of grace, for it is by grace that we are saved and again it is by grace that our works can bear fruit for eternal life;”58

c) a catechesis oriented to the sacraments. “Attentive to the norms established by the diocesan bishop, a pastor is to take care in a special way:

that suitable catechesis is imparted for the celebration of the sacraments;

that through catechetical instruction imparted for an appropriate period of time children are prepared properly for the first reception of the Sacraments of Penance and the Most Holy Eucharist and for the Sacrament of Confirmation.”59

“d) a catechesis of the beatitudes, for the way of Christ is summed up in the beatitudes, the only path that leads to the eternal beatitude for which the human heart longs;

“e) a catechesis of sin and forgiveness, for unless man acknowledges that he is a sinner he cannot know the truth about himself, which is a condition for acting justly; and without the offer of forgiveness he would not be able to bear this truth;

“f) a catechesis of the human virtues which causes one to grasp the beauty and attraction of right dispositions towards goodness;

“g) a catechesis of the Christian virtues of faith, hope, and charity, generously inspired by the example of the saints;

“h) a catechesis of the twofold commandment of charity set forth in the Decalogue.”60 “Before his Passion, Christ, interrogated by an expert of the Law about was the greatest and first commandment, said: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; this is the greatest and first commandment (Mt 22:38). And certainly it is the greatest, most noble and useful of all the commandments… then in this is fulfilled all the commandments.”61 “Two are the roots of all the commandments…: The love of God and of neighbor.”62

“i) an ecclesial catechesis, for it is through the manifold exchanges of “spiritual goods” in the “communion of saints” that Christian life can grow, develop, and be communicated.”63

“The first and last point of reference of this catechesis will always be Jesus Christ himself, who is "the way, and the truth, and the life (Jn 14:6).”64 The fact of Jesus Christ as the fullness of revelation is the foundation of the christocentrism of catechesis: the Mystery of Christ, in the revealed message, is not merely an element most joined to others but the central element, apart from which the remaining elements are ordered and illumined. “It is by looking to Him in faith that Christ’s faithful can hope that He Himself fulfills His promises in them, and that, by loving Him with the same love with which He has loved them, they may perform works in keeping with their dignity.”65

“I ask you to consider that our Lord Jesus Christ is your true head, and that you are one of his members. He belongs to you as the head belongs to its members; all that is his is yours: his spirit, his heart, his body and soul, and all his faculties. You must make use of all these as of your own, to serve, praise, love, and glorify God. You belong to him, as members belong to their head. And so he longs for you to use all that is in you, as if it were his own, for the service and glory of the Father.”66 In the same way, each Christian would be able to say with St. Paul: “For to me, to live is Christ”67

Conclusion

Above all, Charity. To conclude this presentation it is opportune to remember the pastoral principle that the Roman Catechism enunciated: “… as our Lord and Savior has not only declared, but has also proved by his own example, that ‘the Law and the Prophets depend on love,’ and as, according to the Apostle, charity is the end of the commandments, and the fulfillment of the law, it is unquestionably a paramount duty of the pastor, to use the utmost assiduity to excite the faithful to a love of the infinite goodness of God towards us; that burning with a sort of divine ardor, they may be powerfully attracted to the supreme and all perfect good, to adhere to which is true and solid happiness, as is fully experienced by him who can say with the Prophet; ‘What have I in heaven but thee? And besides thee what do I desire upon earth?’ This, assuredly, is that more excellent way pointed out by the Apostle, when he refers all his doctrines and instructions to ‘charity which never faileth;’ for whatever is proposed by the pastor, whether it be the exercise of faith, of hope, or of some moral virtue; the love of God should be so strongly insisted upon by him, as to show clearly that all the works of perfect Christian virtue can have no other origin and no other end than divine love.”68
